title: The Effects of Lighting Design on Mood, Attention, and Stress

findings.quote: Total Mood Disturbance was not significantly different across light condition, F(2, 10) = 0.55, p = .58.

stimuli.description: Three lighting conditions: 1) bright, white light (10,000 lux, 6500°K, full-spectrum, SAD lamp), 2) dim, blue light (40 lux, 450 nm), 3) dim, warm incandescent light (40 lux, 3500°K, control).

Visual stimuli for Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT) consisting of 16 possible combinations of four shapes (square, circle, triangle, star) and four colors (red, blue, green, yellow). Target was a red square, presented for 100ms with randomized blank periods (1000ms, 1500ms, 2000ms, or 2500ms).

limitations: Small sample size (N=11) potentially leading to insufficient statistical power to detect genuine differences.
Experimental procedures may not have been sensitive enough or were flawed.
Presence of extraneous variables (e.g., weather patterns, time of day, time of semester/academic workload) may have affected data quality and increased variability.

The specific type of attention measured by the CCPT (sustained attention) might not be the type most affected by lighting conditions; other forms like multitasking or suppression of distraction might be more relevant.
The POMS-SF measure might not have been sensitive enough to detect minor mood changes, or its subscales (e.g., 'Confusion', 'Anger') were irrelevant to lighting effects.
Participants might have remembered and tried to maintain consistency with their previous responses on the POMS-SF.
Some adjectives in the POMS-SF were closely related or unfamiliar to participants (e.g., 'Bushed'), potentially reducing the measure's specificity and accuracy.
Heart rate might not have fully captured physiological arousal as effectively as other measures (e.g., skin conductance, cortisol), and was easily influenced by the researcher's presence.

The possibility of a genuine null effect, suggesting that lighting conditions may not affect the measured constructs, and previous literature might have erroneously reported effects due to methodological flaws.
Subjective preferences for certain lighting conditions might have influenced participants' emotional states more than the direct physiological effects of light.
The sample did not predominantly include participants with Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD), which might have reduced the likelihood of observing changes in mood, attention, and stress.
